idiom_name: require/ensuring preconditions plus Either/Option results instead of early return
implementation_notes: Scala can write the classic guard, but the expression-oriented culture treats return as a last resort: closures cannot return locally, if/else and match are expressions, and the idiomatic replacements are Predef.require(cond, message) for caller preconditions - its API page states that on failure the caller is to blame, unlike assert - ensuring for postconditions, and Either[Error, A] / Option[A] results computed by an expression so the failure travels in the type. Early return is still justified in imperative algorithm code where restructuring to an expression would obscure it; the guard then reads best as a small named check at the top of the body.
code_sketch:
def publish(draft: Draft): Either[String, Published] =
  require(draft.body.nonEmpty, "body required")      // guard: caller's fault
  if draft.readyAt.isAfter(clock.now) then
    Left("not ready")                                // typed early exit
  else
    Right(repo.publish(draft))                       // expression is the happy path
pitfalls: require throws IllegalArgumentException, so it never appears in the signature; callers see a runtime failure where an Either would have typed it.
return inside a lambda or for-comprehension body is a non-local return (deprecated in Scala 3 and implemented with exceptions); use an expression, a match, or a scoped boundary instead.
require and assert carry different blame: require blames the caller, assert signals an internal defect; swapping them makes failure messages lie.
